content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposed a new idea of pretraining Enc-Dec model for low-resource Machine Translation. The authors build a synthetic parallel data with ‘nonsense’words and their corresponding upper cases. 
Finetuning from such pretrained models greatly cut down the toxicity rate in translated scripts, as compared to finetuning from real-sentence pretrained models, e.g. M2M. For some translation pairs, the proposed method obtained competitive BLEU score with M2M, but for some pairs, it shows deficiency either M2M or Baseline.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 
1. The idea of utilizing self-construct words as synthetic data sounds novel and cool. It may be another road of combining Pretrained Language Model and Machine Translation.
2. In terms of reducing toxicity in Pretrained Language Models, this work has successfully fulfilled the goal.
Weaknesses:
1. The experiments(Figure 2) demonstrating the motivation has some problems. First of all, I didn’t find any description to the BASELINE, but only “this baseline” from section 4.2. Second, you should better present the BLEU score of Transformer-Base(31.87), which is higher than all your results in Fig 2 (but you write “benefit” in the paper). Third, each real-world word matching a unique “nonsense” word means there still exists certain alignments between source and target sentences(statistically), which may help translation. But in section 4.3, how well can synthetic parallel data benefit translation without such premise is a big question. Fourth, you obviously forgot to label the graphs with “WMT2014 DE-EN”.
2. Two experiments are unreproducible(Former 2 pairs in Table 1).For my-en, the data website is currently unavailable. For id-en, the data are filtered by unmentioned method, and are divided into train, dev and test sets with unknown rule, or random seed. Notably, the third experiment on WMT17 TR-EN shows the proposed method is worse than random-initialized model. How can readers believe that this method really works?
3. The tokenization is confusing. This paper used sentencepiece model from XLMR, based on real-world language. On one hand, synthetic tokens may contain subwords that never exist in the sentencepiece model(such as: yxm, wtq). On the other hand, the hypothesized alignment(like: she <-> SHE) will impair word embedding table, since “she” in English should align with “sie” in Germany.
4. I can’t find any dataset scale information for Table 4.
5. Since parameter quantities of M2M and FLORES models are listed in Table 4, why are other parameter quantities missing?
6. When calculating Toxicity rate, it is not solely on test sets, but the combination of test sets and 100k sentences sampled from CC-100. I find no explanation for the additional datasets and I worry if those 100k sentences were selected rather than randomly sampled. If this problem is not clearly explained, the success on reducing toxicity is also skeptical.
7. In the last paragraph of section 5.1, it writes Table 7, but there is no Table 7 throughout the whole paper.
8. Typos like “transition” in section 5.2 (which should be “translation”).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Poor clarity: Because it failed to introduce the notion of BASELINE(see weaknesses 2). There are also many ambiguous descriptions of the experiments.
Poor quality:  With some concerns for experiments mentioned in Weaknesses, I am not sure if this method really works.
Good novelty: It is a trailblazing work that pretrains language model on synthetic parallel data.
Reproducibility: Terrible. Unavailable dataset website. Self-filtered datasets. No introduction of used datasets(Table 4, de-en).
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposed a great hypothesis that synthetic data could benefit pretrained language model. However, there are big problems on reproducibility and the experimental results are not convincing. The writing is not good with a lot of careless errors and missing information.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper studies two approaches to generate synthetic pretraining data for machine translation. The first method (obfuscated) is taking a real parallel dataset and replacing the tokens by mapping it 1:1 to some randomly-generated (nonsense) tokens. The second method (synthetic) is using a set of rules to generate purely synthetic data. The set of rules include 1. identity (two sentences are the same) 2. case mapping with random deletion and insertion 3. apply synchronous context free grammar on randomly generated source sentence to obtain the target sentence.

The paper presents analysis in low-resource machine translation to show that both obfuscated and synthetic pre-training techniques can mitigate the issue of hallucinated model toxicity while maintaining certain performance benefits of the pretraining procedure.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
1. The paper studies an interesting setup where the pre-training data does not contain real words but maintains some properties of the language or the language pair.
2. The paper conducts detailed experiments to verify how useful the obfuscated and synthetic pretraining are.
3. The synthetic pretraining data technique could be used to study the usefulness of a certain property of the pretraining data, not limit to the rules proposed by the paper.

Weaknesses
1. The experiments are being done only in low-resource setting. I would expect more reasoning to justify the choice of the setting. I could imagine that one reason is that the pretraining matters more in the low-resource setting. I also acknowledge that in Figure 2 we can see that the gap between baseline and from scratch becomes smaller and smaller when the finetuning data increases.
2. In the low-resource setting where the finetuning set consists of only 20k or 50k. It seems the drop from the baseline is large. Where these experiments are still interesting to see, it might be as appealing in practice as developer might not want to sacrifice the performance. No concrete feedback, but I do appreciate that the authors present the full view of the analysis.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is written clearly and easy to follow. I believe the experiments can be reproduced.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents an interesting setting. The setup might be more extreme than what would be considered in practice, but the experiments show interesting findings that helps with our understanding with pretraining and might indicate future direction.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors show that pre-training on obfuscated data and synthetic tasks also help transfer benefits to a downstream translation task. They show that inner layers of the models (and not the embeddings) are responsible for transfer learning). Even with very high rates of obfuscation, transfer benefits are seen. Synthetic pre-training is also shown to generate less toxic output compared to pre-training on true text data.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

- This work though validates the previous work on pre-training with synthetic tasks. 
- The paper suggests a new synthetic task that captures reordering and long-distance dependency and the results look promising.  
- The paper also shows that synthetic pre-training can reduce catastrophic mistranslations compared to pre-training on natural language text.

**Weaknesses**

- Previous work (Aji et al 2020) has shown the role of inner layers in transfer learning, as well as the ability of synthetic tasks to accomplish transfer learning. This paper should be cited in related work. Hence, the novelty of the work is limited.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarifications Needed**

- A different set of languages is used for evaluation of the obfuscated and synthetic pre-training scenarios. A comparison on the same set of languages would help to compare the two approaches as well. 

**Originality**

- Some major findings of the work have also been reported in previous work [1] in the context of NMT.

1. Alham Fikri Aji, Nikolay Bogoychev, Kenneth Heafield, Rico Sennrich. In neural machine translation, what does transfer learning transfer?. ACL 2020.  (https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.688/)
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper studies the role of pre-training via the use of obfuscated & synthetic datasets for neural machine translation. The major findings regarding the role of pre-training and utility of synthetic datasets have been addressed in previous work. The utility of synthetic datasets in reducing toxicity in MT output is an interesting contribution.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies a variety of methods for pre-training NMT models on obfuscated or fully-synthetic data. The authors show that such methods can approach the performance of conventional pre-training on large parallel corpora, while also reducing toxicity. The paper proposes a variety of obfuscation techniques and procedures for creating synthetic data, and compare them against (1) training from scratch or (2) pre-training a NMT model on a modest amount of German-English data.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Interesting research question
- Thorough experimental setup, with a variety of conditions considered.

Weaknesses:
- The pre-training baselines seem a bit weak to me---3.5 German/English pairs is not really that much. How do the results look if you do something that's a bit more standard? Is there an off the shelf model that you can look at here? In general, it'd be nice to understand how these results change as a function of amount of pre-training data (since, as the authors noted, this is conventionally pretty easy to mine).

Questions:
- How come the models seem to be more toxic on de-id in general? (table 4)
- What is the obfuscation ratio in Section 5.2?

Comments:
- Figures would be _much_ more readable if they had X and Y axes. They're pretty interpretable after reading the prose, but it would still greatly aid readability if the figures were made a bit more stand-alone. For example, there are a bunch of comparisons going on in Figure 2 and 3, and it'd be nice to be able to focus on understanding what those are rather than deciphering which bar corresponds to which different condition.
- I think a lot of the motivation around privacy requires 100% (or very nearly 100%) obfuscation, but it isn't clear that synthetic pre-training is effective in this setting. For example, looking at figure 2, pre-training on 100% obfuscation is only slightly better than no pre-training at all. I feel like there's a bit of a mismatch between this motivation and the actual results / implied impact of the results.
- I think the NLP community shares the intuition that translation is a rather "shallow" task, and that you can do quite well by just translating word-by-word. It'd be nice to see some discussion of this---are synthetic pre-training approaches more suited for "shallower" downstream tasks in particular?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I thought the paper was reasonably clear, excepting the comments I made about the figures. The work is thorough and explores a variety of settings, which I appreciated. It represents another entry in a growing body of work on synthetic data for pre-training, so while the idea is not entirely novel, the setting for MT is new.

The paper mentions in the introduction that "Our goal in this paper is to understand what makes for a good pre-trained model when using synthetic resources.", and I think this is a pretty big overclaim / grandiose goal. It's not clear to me from this paper what makes a good pre-trained model when using a synthetic resources _for the case of MT_, let alone in general.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper contributes a study on synthetic pre-training data for NMT, adding to a growing body of work on synthetic pre-training. The authors thoroughly explore a variety of experimental settings and propose several methods for synthetic or obfuscated pre-training. My main concern is that the comparisons to the baselines are quite weak. NMT pre-training data is generally much larger than what was used here, and it'd be nice to see a comparison to "real" baselines. While the ideas are promising, it isn't clear to me that this holds in the generally-seen settings. On the other hand, this paper could contribute a better understanding of the principles behind effective synthetic pre-training data, but I didn't really come away with a good sense of this.

content.title: Synthetic Pre-Training Tasks for Neural Machine Translation
content.abstract: Pre-training is an effective technique for ensuring robust performance on a variety of machine learning tasks. It typically depends on large-scale crawled corpora that can result in toxic or biased models. Such data can also be problematic with respect to copyright, attribution, and privacy. Pre-training with synthetic tasks and data is a promising way of alleviating such concerns since no real-world information is ingested by the model. Our goal in this paper is to understand what makes for a good pre-trained model when using synthetic resources. We answer this question in the context of neural machine translation by considering two novel approaches to translation model pre-training. Our first approach studies the effect of pre-training on obfuscated data derived from a parallel corpus by mapping words to a vocabulary of `nonsense' tokens. Our second approach explores the effect of pre-training on procedurally generated synthetic parallel data that does not depend on any real human language corpus. Our empirical evaluation on multiple language pairs shows that, to a surprising degree, the benefits of pre-training can be realized even with obfuscated or purely synthetic parallel data. In our analysis, we consider the extent to which obfuscated and synthetic pre-training techniques can be used to mitigate the issue of hallucinated model toxicity.
